title: Inna and Its Sisters — First Look (إِنَّ / أَنَّ)

steps.title: كَانَ's mirror image
body: You already know كَانَ shifts a nominal sentence's predicate to accusative, leaving the subject nominative. إنّ وأخواتها ("inna and its sisters") is a family of particles that does the reverse: it pushes the SUBJECT to accusative and leaves the predicate nominative. الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ ("the house is big") becomes إِنَّ الْبَيْتَ كَبِيرٌ ("indeed the house is big") — الْبَيْتُ's ـُ becomes ـَ; كَبِيرٌ never changes.

إِنَّ opens a sentence for emphasis ("indeed, truly") — it's the family's namesake and most common member. أَنَّ does the same case-shifting job, but instead of standing alone it subordinates a whole nominal clause as "that" after a verb of saying, hearing, or knowing: سَمِعْتُ أَنَّ الطَّقْسَ جَمِيلٌ — "I heard that the weather is beautiful." Don't confuse أَنَّ with أَنْ, an unrelated word (the subjunctive "to") that introduces a verb instead — that one is a separate topic for later.

You've actually known a third sister since your very first weeks: لِأَنَّ ("because") is just لِ + أَنَّ, and it obeys exactly the same rule — the noun right after it goes accusative too. Four more sisters exist (as if, a heavier "but," perhaps, would that) and are saved for a later lesson.

steps.title: Three sentences, one family
steps.intro: Read each sentence and watch what happens to the noun right after إِنَّ, أَنَّ, or لِأَنَّ. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: The case shift
steps.prompt: الطَّقْسَ ends in a fatḥa here, not the ḍamma you'd expect on a plain topic. Why?

options.label: It is إِنَّ's subject, which إِنَّ pushes to accusative
It is the object of a hidden verb
It is an iḍāfa's first term, so it drops its own ending

steps.explanation: إِنَّ (and every one of its sisters) pushes the noun right after it to accusative — the mirror image of what كَانَ does to the predicate instead of the subject.

steps.title: That vs. to
steps.explanation: This lesson's أَنَّ (double ن) subordinates a full nominal clause as "that." A different, unrelated word — أَنْ, single ن, the subjunctive "to" — introduces a verb instead; the two are easy to mix up in translit but not in meaning.

steps.title: A word you already knew
steps.prompt: لِأَنَّ has been in your vocabulary since A1. What is it actually built from?

options.label: لِ ("for") + أَنَّ — so it follows the same accusative-subject rule
A single, unanalyzable word with no internal structure

steps.explanation: لِأَنَّ is transparently لِ + أَنَّ, so الطَّقْسَ right after it takes the same accusative ending you just saw after إِنَّ and أَنَّ. It is unrelated to لَكِنْ ("but," no shadda, does not shift case).

steps.title: You've met three sisters
steps.message: إِنَّ, أَنَّ, and the already-known لِأَنَّ — three members of إنّ وأخواتها, all pushing the following noun to accusative, the mirror image of كَانَ. Four more sisters and the attached-pronoun forms are still ahead.
